meeting_header: Date: 2027-08-03 | Start: 15:00 PDT | Duration: 48m | Recorded: yes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Connor (Redwood SE), Aisha (NovusGears Head of Security), Ben (Platform Eng), Liam (CISO)
summary: Discovery focused on security posture requirements for NovusGears' planned inference deployment. Key topics: SOC 2/ISO evidence, SSO via SAML, RBAC granular controls, audit log retention/export, customer-managed KMS and encryption, and trade-offs between Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Agreed next steps: send SOC2 artifacts, demo BYOK flow, schedule SE deep-dive.
topics: SOC 2 Type II scope and evidence
RBAC and least privilege model mapping
Audit logs retention/export and SIEM integration
Encryption: at-rest and in-transit, BYOK/HSM options
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private trade-offs and costs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya Patel, AE on the account, and Connor Li our SE is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Aisha Khan: Hi Maya, good thanks. Liam and Ben are here too. We wanted to focus on security and hosting assumptions, especially around KMS and audit logs.
[00:15] Connor Li: Awesome, we'll keep it security-first. Quick agenda — run through SOC2/ISO evidence, SSO, RBAC, logs, and show how Redwood handles BYOK in Private and what Dedicated offers. Is that ok?
[00:23] Liam O'Neill: Yep, perfect. We're primarily evaluating three paths — Redwood Hosted for speed, Dedicated for performance controls, and Private for full network and key isolation.
[00:32] Ben Torres: Just to add, our platform currently encrypts everything with customer keys in KMS and we require ability to rotate keys and get attestations.
[00:39] Maya Patel: Totally. Quick housekeeping — we'll share links after the call: SOC2 summary, DPA, and a short runbook for onboard. I'll drop those in the follow-up. Connor, want to start SOC2?
[00:48] Connor Li: Sure. Redwood is SOC 2 Type II for our hosted control plane — that covers our operational controls, change management, availability, confidentiality — standard. For Private deployments, customers run a private control plane so the compliance boundary shifts. We can provide the SOC2 report for the hosted service and a mapping for Private to show how controls are met on your side. (slight pause) Note: sometimes the transcript system mislabels our "Redwood Private" mention as "private package" in notes.
[01:12] Aisha Khan: When you say "mapping" — do you provide a gap assessment or just a controls matrix?
[01:18] Connor Li: We provide a controls matrix that maps Redwood controls to typical customer controls, and for larger engagements we do a brief gap analysis + recommended mitigations. For example, if you require all EKM/HSM attestation on-prem we document steps to satisfy auditor expectations.
[01:30] Liam O'Neill: We need explicit language around data residency for several EU customers. Can logs and data be pinned to eu-west-1 and retained according to our retention policy?
[01:39] Maya Patel: Yes — Hosted supports region pinning for data residency. For audit logs, we can export logs to your S3 in region of choice. Retention policies are configurable; we can retain logs for X days by default and export to your archive for longer retention.
[01:52] Ben Torres: What's X? (laughs) We usually require seven years for certain records.
[01:55] Connor Li: Right, default is shorter — typically 90 days in the console — but we have export pipelines so you can ship raw audit logs to your bucket for 7+ years. We'll share the export playbook.
[02:06] Aisha Khan: Ok good. Next, SSO. We use enterprise SAML and SCIM for provisioning. How mature is Redwood's SAML/SCIM implementation?
[02:13] Maya Patel: SSO is generally supported across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. SAML for auth and SCIM for user provisioning is available; we also support IdP-initiated and SP-initiated flows. Connor can add specifics on attributes.
[02:23] Connor Li: Attributes, yeah. We map groups to RBAC roles, and SCIM syncs group membership. There have been occasional customer notes where group names mismatch — transcription misreads group as "grime" sometimes — but we send a mapping doc you can validate before roll-out.
[02:36] Liam O'Neill: For RBAC we need least privilege role definitions: admin, ops, viewer, model-deployer, billing. How granular does Redwood go?
[02:44] Connor Li: We have a policy-based RBAC engine. Out of the box: Admin, Editor, Viewer. But for enterprise we support custom roles (e.g., model-deployer) with fine-grained permissions scoped by project and model. We also support attribute-based access controls if you want to build rules off SCIM attributes.
[02:58] Ben Torres: Can we integrate with our internal IAM to get service-to-service tokens? We don't want long-lived API keys floating around.
[03:05] Maya Patel: Yes — we support short-lived tokens via our token service and can integrate with your ID broker. For Dedicated and Private we also support workload identity federation so you can mint tokens from your own cluster.
[03:16] Aisha Khan: On to KMS — our auditors insist on customer-managed keys for any PII. Do you support BYOK and HSM-backed keys in Hosted or only Private?
[03:26] Connor Li: Good question. Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer-provided KMS in certain enterprise tiers — basically you configure your cloud KMS (GCP/AWS/Azure) and we use keys for envelope encryption. For full HSM-attested BYOK where you want the key never leaving your control, Private is the recommended path: you deploy a private control plane and bring your own HSM or KMS. We also have Dedicated with optional VPC peering and KMS integration for stricter isolation.
[03:50] Liam O'Neill: So for the BYOK flow we'll need a demo of the key rotation and proof-of-rotation. Can you show us key rotation logs and attestations?
[03:58] Connor Li: Yep. We'll show the rotation flow and how audit events are emitted for key ops. We'll also demo how keys are rotated without any data re-encryption on the fly due to envelope keys. I'll include sample audit lines in the benchmark sheet.
[04:10] Ben Torres: How about network egress — if we pick Private, does Redwood run any cloud connectors that leak traffic outside our VPC?
[04:18] Connor Li: For Private, no outbound control plane traffic goes through Redwood's shared network — it's customer-controlled. For Dedicated we offer an option: you can enable egress lock-down via NAT gateways and restrict endpoints. We'll share the architecture doc.
[04:30] Aisha Khan: Audit logs — what is captured? HTTP requests, token usage, model inference logs? We want to be careful about payloads containing PII.
[04:39] Maya Patel: Good nuance. We capture control-plane events (API calls, token issuance, role changes), and by default inference payloads are not logged in full — we capture metadata and truncated request IDs to trace requests. For customers who want full inference logs for debugging we can export them but we'd recommend redaction or hashing of PII fields before export.
[04:58] Liam O'Neill: Does Redwood have an out-of-the-box SIEM integration?
[05:02] Connor Li: We have native connectors to common SIEMs via log export to S3, and we support streaming to Splunk/Datadog via Kinesis or HTTP forwarders. There's a small config step in Dedicated/Private to set up log forwarders.
[05:14] Ben Torres: Encryption in transit — do you terminate TLS at your load balancer in Hosted? We prefer mutual TLS.
[05:19] Connor Li: In Hosted we terminate TLS at our edge, but we support mTLS termination options on Dedicated and Private where you can apply your certs and require mTLS between services.
[05:29] Maya Patel: Quick check — any legal/procurement constraints we should know now? Contracts, SLAs, or export controls?
[05:35] Liam O'Neill: We'll need a standard enterprise SLA and export control clause for some APAC customers. Also question: is the data processing addendum (DPA) compatible with standard EU regs?
[05:43] Maya Patel: Yes, our DPA is GDPR-aligned. I'll include the DPA and the standard SLA in the follow-up. If you need changes we can have Legal review it for enterprise terms.
[05:52] Aisha Khan: One more: tamper-evident audit logs. Do you provide integrity proofs or chain-of-custody for logs?
[05:58] Connor Li: We provide log signing and can enable hashing of log batches before export. For ultra-sensitive customers we recommend piping logs to your own WORM storage and enabling hashing+signature verification on ingest. We'll include an example flow in the artifact link.
[06:12] Ben Torres: Regarding Dedicated vs Hosted cost trade-off — can you quantify overhead for dedicated KMS and higher perf?
[06:18] Maya Patel: High-level: Dedicated includes reserved capacity and optional dedicated KMS integration; cost depends on GPU type and reserved commit. We'll provide a back-of-envelope cost comparison in the follow-up pricing sheet. For Private, there's a platform fee plus deployment/ops cost.
[06:29] Liam O'Neill: Are there example customers with similar compliance needs you can name?
[06:33] Maya Patel: Off the top: a payments customer and a health-tech customer — I'll share anonymized references and case studies. Sometimes the transcript system munges names, I'll make sure the links are correct.
[06:43] Aisha Khan: On delegation — we want an approver workflow for model deploys. Can RBAC be tied to approvals so a deploy requires sign-off from a specific group?
[06:50] Connor Li: Yes — you can gate certain actions behind approvals. We support webhooks for approval flows, and role-based gating. We'll share a sample policy YAML that shows how to require approver group membership for deploys.
[07:02] Ben Torres: For audit timeline — when you export logs, is there any window where logs might be delayed? We want near-real-time ingestion to our SIEM.
[07:10] Connor Li: There can be small batching delays for export (1-2 minutes typical), but for streaming we can get near real-time via Kinesis or HTTP forwarders. We'll show latencies in the benchmark doc.
[07:20] Maya Patel: Ok I think that's the crux. Anything else on the security side?
[07:23] Liam O'Neill: One last nit — retention of artifacts: models, embeddings, KV cache. Do you retain KV cache between restarts? How is that stored?
[07:32] Connor Li: KV cache is in-memory for inference nodes, but we persist snapshots optionally to object storage for warm starts. We can configure TTLs and retention. We'll share the KV cache lifecycle doc; sometimes 'KV' is transcribed as 'K V cash' which is amusing.
[07:43] Aisha Khan: (laughs) noted. Ok, next steps?
[07:46] Maya Patel: I'll drop SOC2 summary, DPA, SLA, and references. Connor will spin up a demo with BYOK and show audit exports + RBAC mapping. Let's tentatively schedule the SE deep-dive week of Aug 16. Does that work?
[07:58] Ben Torres: Works for me.
[08:01] Liam O'Neill: Works.
[08:03] Aisha Khan: Great. Thanks both.
[47:15] Maya Patel: Cool thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts. (call ends)
